title: The pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
hook: servants given money to trade while the master is away

segments.voice: Yesterday, a publican at the back of the Temple asked for mercy and went home justified. Your line was be merciful to me. Did you say it instead of comparing? Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Jesus is nearly at Jerusalem now. He's just been to Jericho, where a short tax collector named Zacheus climbed a sycamore to see him. The crowd is buzzing. Luke says they thought the kingdom of God was about to appear immediately, any minute now, as soon as they reached the city. So Jesus tells them a story about waiting. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and come back. Before he leaves, he calls ten servants and hands each one the same small sum of money. Today, the pounds.
screen: `NEARLY AT JERUSALEM.` → `THE KINGDOM, ANY MINUTE NOW.` → `A STORY ABOUT WAITING.`

segments.voice: Each servant gets one pound. The Greek word is mina: a real sum of money, though the master will later call it a little. And the instruction is two words in the Douay: "Trade till I come." Then the master's citizens send a message after him: we will not have this man to reign over us. Some readers hear an echo there: Josephus tells of a son of Herod who went to Rome to have his rule confirmed, with a delegation following to oppose him. The master comes back a king anyway and calls in his servants. The first: your pound has gained ten pounds. "Well done, good servant, because thou hast been faithful in a little, thou shalt have power over ten cities." The second has made five, and gets five cities. Then a third comes with his pound wrapped in a napkin. I was afraid of you, he says, because you're an austere man. You take up what you didn't lay down. So I kept it safe. The master's answer is sharp: then why didn't you at least put it in the bank? The pound is taken from him and given to the one who has ten. Notice what the third servant got wrong. He didn't steal. He didn't waste. He just never used it, because he was afraid. Everyone started with the same pound. The difference was what they did with it while the master was away. Some Catholic readers take the pound as what everyone receives alike: faith, the word, the life of grace. Elsewhere Matthew tells a similar parable with talents, different amounts to each. Luke's version says: you all got the same gift. Trade with it.
screen: `ONE POUND EACH, THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `WE WILL NOT HAVE THIS MAN.` · `FAITHFUL IN A LITTLE.` · `WRAPPED IN A NAPKIN, OUT OF FEAR.` · then, large: `TRADE TILL I COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use one gift you've buried. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're good at, or something you were given, that you've kept wrapped in a napkin. A voice you don't sing with anymore. A language you stopped speaking. A skill you're afraid to be seen trying. Patience, humor, a knack for fixing things. Pick one. Notice the fear that keeps it wrapped. Then picture unwrapping it once this week, for someone else. If you pray, thank God for the gift. The bell holds the time.
The pounds. Ten servants, one coin each, told to trade until the master returns; the one who buried his out of fear loses it. Today's word.

Your line: trade with it. Unwrap one buried gift this week. And that's week sixty-eight: count the cost, the clever steward, Lazarus, one came back, the persistent widow, the publican, and the pounds. Day four hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of the gifts given to every baptized person and of using them in service, and some parishes ask members to share their gifts, from music to accounting to visiting the sick.

fork.setup: your master has left you one pound and gone to a far country. you think he's a hard man. what do you do?
options: trade with it and take the risk.
wrap it in a napkin and keep it safe.
put it in the bank for interest.
fork.reveal: the third servant hides it out of fear. the master says even the bank would have been better, and gives his pound to the one who has ten.

original.note: Greek: mina, a sum of money; the Douay translates it pound.

trapdoor: what you thought: the pounds is a story about investing money wisely.
what it means: everyone receives the same gift; faithfulness means using it while the master is away, not burying it out of fear.
what a scholar hears: a nobleman who travels to receive a kingdom, opposed by his own citizens, echoes Josephus's account of Archelaus going to Rome after Herod's death.
